stamps.test: replication on real PostgreSQL > replay_lag: a long transaction on a follower holds up replay (followers-run-behind)

stamps.note: Ran it on PostgreSQL 14.15: on a follower that was behind, the check returned false and a read there showed the old balance; once it passed her LSN, the read included the deposit.
stamps.test: replication on real PostgreSQL > a lagging follower returns the balance from before the deposit (where-did-my-deposit-go, read-your-own-writes)

stamps.note: Ran it on PostgreSQL 14.15: with db2's replay paused, a commit still returned once db2 had the entry on disk (a read there still showed the old balance). remote_apply waited for the replay; local didn't wait at all.
stamps.test: replication on real PostgreSQL > synchronous_commit: on waits for the flush, remote_apply for the replay, local for nobody (who-waits-for-whom)

stamps.note: Ran it on PostgreSQL 14.15: with the only sync standby crashed, commits waited in SyncRep with no error and all finished when it came back. Cancelling one printed that warning word for word.
stamps.test: replication on real PostgreSQL > the only sync follower crashes: commits wait with no error, then finish (when-the-sync-follower-dies)

stamps.note: Ran it on PostgreSQL 14.15: db2 was sync and db3 potential; when db2 crashed, db3 took over and commits kept flowing; with both down, commits waited. With ANY 1, one follower was enough.
stamps.test: replication on real PostgreSQL > FIRST 1 (db2, db3) and ANY 1: who the leader waits for (one-sync-rest-async)

stamps.note: Ran it on PostgreSQL 14.15: after the leader crashed, the follower that had received the most log was promoted, and it replayed what it had received but not yet applied.
stamps.test: replication on real PostgreSQL > the leader crashes: promote the most complete follower, lose the unshipped writes, fence the old leader (who-takes-over, writes-that-vanish, split-brain, fencing)

stamps.note: Ran it on PostgreSQL 14.15: the pg_rewind line threw away the writes nobody else had, and the old leader came back as a read-only follower of db-2. (The pcs line needs Pacemaker and wasn't run.)
stamps.test: replication on real PostgreSQL > the leader crashes: promote the most complete follower, lose the unshipped writes, fence the old leader (who-takes-over, writes-that-vanish, split-brain, fencing)

stamps.note: Ran it on MySQL 9.2.0: with two leaders replicating to each other, us-east handed out 1, 3, 5 and eu-west (offset 2) 2, 4, 6. Both ended up with all six rows and no collisions.
stamps.test: replication: the MySQL lines > two leaders hand out odd and even IDs (multi-leader)

stamps.note: Ran it on MySQL 9.2.0: while a long transaction on the replica held up the applier, Seconds_Behind_Source climbed past 2, then fell back to 0.
stamps.test: replication: the MySQL lines > SHOW REPLICA STATUS: Seconds_Behind_Source while replay is held up (followers-run-behind)

stamps.note: Ran it on MySQL 9.2.0: commits waited for the replica's ack; with the replica stopped, one commit waited out the 10 s timeout, then the source fell back to async until the replica returned.
stamps.test: replication: the MySQL lines > semi-sync waits for a replica, then falls back to async after the timeout (one-sync-rest-async)

stamps.note: Ran it on PostgreSQL 14.15: with these lines and an empty standby.signal, the replica served reads, refused writes, and after replaying the primary's inserts its orders table was exactly as big as the primary's.
stamps.test: sharding on real PostgreSQL > a replica is a full copy that replays every write (copies-dont-add-room)

stamps.note: Ran it on PostgreSQL 14.15: with four shard databases and the lesson's users split by first letter, shard-0 answered alice | frank.
stamps.test: sharding on real PostgreSQL > every shard runs the same schema but holds a different slice (split-the-rows)

stamps.note: Ran it on PostgreSQL 14.15: with orders hash-partitioned four ways on customer_id (partitions standing in for shards), the first query touched 1 partition and the report all 4.
stamps.test: sharding on real PostgreSQL > a query with the shard key touches one shard, anything else all of them (what-hashing-costs, keep-related-together, pick-a-key)

stamps.note: Ran it on PostgreSQL 14.15: with the lesson's tenants loaded, acme's lookup returned 0, the UPDATE changed exactly one row, and no other tenant moved.
stamps.test: sharding on real PostgreSQL > moving one tenant is one UPDATE (directory)

stamps.note: Ran it on PostgreSQL 14.15: over four shards of very different sizes, the merged sums and counts gave exactly avg(total) of all rows; averaging the averages was far off.
stamps.test: sharding on real PostgreSQL > merge partial sums, don’t average the averages (scatter-gather)

stamps.note: Ran it on PostgreSQL 14.15: on two shards, after PREPARE the coordinator disconnected; both transactions stayed prepared (even across a shard restart) and writes to the two rows waited until COMMIT PREPARED.
stamps.test: sharding on real PostgreSQL > two-phase commit: prepared transactions wait, holding their locks (transactions)

stamps.note: Ran it on PostgreSQL 14.15: in two sessions, in the animation's order, both read NULL, both UPDATEs went through, and the row ended up saying bob.
stamps.test: race conditions on real PostgreSQL > seat · check, then book: the animation's interleaving, replayed on PostgreSQL (check-then-act)

stamps.note: Ran it on PostgreSQL 14.15: in two sessions, in the animation's order, the first UPDATE matched 1 row and the second 0.
stamps.test: race conditions on real PostgreSQL > seat · one conditional UPDATE: the animation's interleaving, replayed on PostgreSQL (check-then-act)

stamps.note: Ran it on PostgreSQL 14.15: in two sessions, in the animation's order, both read 100, both passed the check, both wrote 20.
stamps.test: race conditions on real PostgreSQL > bank · no lock: the animation's interleaving, replayed on PostgreSQL (double-spend)

stamps.note: Ran it on PostgreSQL 14.15: in two sessions, in the animation's order, the second SELECT … FOR UPDATE waited for the first COMMIT, then read 20. A plain SELECT didn’t wait.
stamps.test: race conditions on real PostgreSQL > bank · FOR UPDATE: the animation's interleaving, replayed on PostgreSQL (double-spend)

stamps.note: Ran it on PostgreSQL 14.15: in two sessions, in the animation's order, the second UPDATE matched 0 rows; the retry read 20, 8 and stopped.
stamps.test: race conditions on real PostgreSQL > bank · version check: the animation's interleaving, replayed on PostgreSQL (double-spend)
